stories.story_title: UAA students gain a local source of brain-signal data
stories.summary_2_sentences: UAA announced September 9 that its AI and Robotics Lab acquired a DSI-24 EEG through the Educational Legacy Fund. It supports AI/ML research and training; described reading and programming studies remain planned.
stories.why_it_matters_to_alaskans: Builds Alaska research capability and student experience collecting original data.

verified_facts.fact: 19 scalp electrodes, two earclips and three auxiliary inputs.
Vadim Egorov is photographed watching his own electrical brain signals during training.
Planned studies concern cognitive states during reading and brain activity plus eye movements during programming.
Manufacturer documentation identifies a scientific/engineering research instrument, not an FDA-approved diagnostic or therapeutic medical device.

quotation.text: I’m excited to be able to collect my own data for my own tasks
quotation.speaker: Vadim Egorov, graduate student

story_fuel: A student moves from downloading datasets to recording data for his own research questions.
Illustrative visual: headset pickups become traces, then data for analysis.
stories.local_sentiment: Egorov expresses excitement. Faculty welcome interdisciplinary collaboration. These are named participants, not a survey of Alaska opinion; no tribal or disability-community response was found.
stories.status_boundary: Acquisition and training are reported. Successful brain-computer control, diagnostic accuracy, clinical benefit, finalized studies, participant counts and study results are not reported.

manufacturer_context.sampling_rate: 300 Hz, with a 600 Hz upgrade available; UAA installed configuration is unreported.
manufacturer_context.data_output: Manufacturer lists raw CSV and EDF recording via DSI-Streamer.
manufacturer_context.avoid: Do not convert vendor claims of >90% correlation with wet EEG into decoding accuracy or UAA validation.

stories.recommendation: Strongest candidate here. Earned celebratory angle: students gain the means to ask and measure their own questions, with honest future tense for studies.

stories.story_title: Alaska robotics season opens with hardship grants and a way to keep older kits in play
stories.summary_2_sentences: FIRST in Alaska’s September 4 update announces BIOBUZZ kickoff events in Anchorage, Fairbanks and Juneau on September 12. It also offers hardship support, including for veteran teams, and explains continued use of existing LEGO hardware for its local Founders Edition season.
stories.why_it_matters_to_alaskans: A concrete path for school teams to start robotics this fall and seek help with equipment access.

sources.outlet: FIRST in Alaska / Juneau Economic Development Council

verified_facts.fact: September 12 kickoff listed at 8 a.m. AKDT; local events listed for Anchorage, Fairbanks and Juneau.
Hardship grants explicitly include veteran teams this year.
Alaska Founders Edition permits older EV3, NXT and RCX hardware as well as Spike Prime for Challenge.

quotation.text: we will help you find a way to play this season
quotation.speaker: FIRST in Alaska organizer update, addressing teams without a robot

story_fuel: An old kit comes out of a school cupboard and gets another season.
A same-day kickoff with practical access support.
stories.local_sentiment: Organizer commitment to participation is explicit. No independent team or parent reaction was verified.
stories.status_boundary: Do not call these AI deployments or assert rural participation totals. Dates are announced events, not proof each event occurred. Verify local calendar before promoting a specific venue/time.
stories.recommendation: Viable workforce/robotics alternative, weaker than EEG for a science explainer. Quantitative outcomes and attendance unreported.
